summary:
Project NANDA (Network AI Agents in Decentralized Architecture) is an open research initiative from MIT that builds infrastructure for an internet of AI agents, mirroring how the open web was built for documents. Ramesh Raskar frames the current agent ecosystem as analogous to the AOL era of the late 1990s—closed platforms, proprietary stores, and siloed orchestration. The transition ahead requires open infrastructure where agents can discover, transact, and co-learn across organizational boundaries without permissions.

The talk organizes the vision around three layers: discovery, commerce, and the bazaar. The Discovery Layer is addressed through the Nanda Index, which functions like DNS for agents but richer—mapping agent identities to agent cards containing signed agent facts records that describe what an agent does, what tools it uses, who built it, and how to reach it. Resolution is adaptive, routing to the best endpoint based on context. Onboarding supports enterprises via their own domain catalogs, existing websites via DNS AID, and individuals via host39.org.

Maria, a core contributor, defines an agent as a model that uses tools in a loop and highlights Open Claw as a self-hosted agent gateway. Agent hosting options include local execution for full control, general clouds like AWS for enterprise readiness, and Maritime, a platform with sleep-and-wake architecture to reduce idle compute costs for running many agents.

The Bazaar and Commerce layers are primarily explored through Nanda Town, an open-source simulation environment that models the full agentic economy. Nanda Town decomposes the agentic web into twelve components—transport, communication, identity, registry, auth, trust, payments, coordination, negotiation, memory, privacy, and data effects—and runs as a discrete event simulation with scripted agents (tier one) and real AI models (tier two). Experiments include marketplace price negotiation, auctions, voting, consensus, and supply chains. Contributors can implement a single layer, plug it into Nanda Town, and observe interactions with the rest of the network.

sections.title: Introduction and Vision
sections.summary: Ramesh Raskar introduces Project NANDA as open infrastructure for an internet of AI agents. He explains the gap: agents lack shared discovery, portable identity, and open coordination across organizations. He draws the AOL-era analogy, predicting a transition from closed agent platforms to an open agentic web. Three layers are introduced: discovery, commerce, and bazaar.

sections.title: Agent Definition and Open Claw
sections.summary: Maria defines an agent as a model that uses tools in a loop. She introduces Open Claw as a self-hosted agent gateway, emphasizing that open-source self-hosted agents matter for control and transparency. She raises the problem of agents finding each other across different servers and owners, motivating the Nanda Index.

sections.title: Nanda Index: Discovery Layer
sections.summary: Maria details the Nanda Index: agents start with an identity, the index returns an agent card with reachability info. Messages go to a message box that handles access, spam filtering, and queuing. The agent facts record is a signed record for trust. Resolution is adaptive—one agent can have multiple endpoints with private details hidden. Three onboarding paths: enterprise catalogs, DNS AID, and host39.org for individuals.

sections.title: Agent Hosting and Maritime
sections.summary: Agent hosting options are discussed: local for full control, AWS for enterprise, and Maritime for cost-efficient multi-agent hosting with sleep-and-wake architecture so idle agents do not burn compute. The hard problems of the agent web live between agents at scale.

sections.title: Nanda Town: Simulation Environment
sections.summary: Nanda Town is introduced as an open-source sandbox for testing agoric networks. It models discovery, identity, registries, messaging, coordination, and more. Users can see agents on a map, watch messages move, compare protocols, and replay runs. The system decomposes the agoric web into 12 parts and runs as a discrete event simulation with two tiers: scripted agents and real AI models. Experiments include marketplaces, auctions, voting, consensus, and supply chains.

sections.title: Summary and Resources
sections.summary: Project NANDA builds open infrastructure for an internet of AI agents: discovery through the index, commerce through portable identity and trust, and coordination through open protocols, all tested in Nanda Town. The audience is directed to projectnanda.org for papers and latest projects.

evidence.excerpt: Nanda, which stands for network AI agents in a decentralized architecture, is an open research building the infrastructure for an internet of AI agents, the way open web was built for documents.
Agents have no shared way to find each other across vendors, no portable identity or trust that isn't owned by a single platform, and no open way to transact and coordinate across organizations.
The internet is about to host not millions or billions, but eventually trillions of autonomous agents.
This is like the AOL era from the late '90s where it was a closed network.

the agent facts record is what makes discovery trustworthy. It is a signed record that tells other agents who this agent is, what it can do, what it is allowed to touch, who built it, and where to reach it.
